title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 19
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Turning the Night On
passages.text:
A. For most of history the city at night was simply dark, and the response to that was regulation rather than illumination. Curfews, gate closures and requirements that anyone abroad after dark carry a light of their own were the standard arrangement, and they treated darkness as a condition to be managed by restricting movement. Lighting the street itself, at public expense, for everyone, reversed that logic and took several centuries to become normal.

B. The earliest municipal schemes were funded by householders rather than authorities, through obligations to hang a lamp outside a frontage on specified nights. Compliance was uneven and the obligation was resented, which is why the schemes were repeatedly re-enacted. Their significance is not the light they produced, which was negligible, but the establishment of the principle that the street outside a house was a shared responsibility rather than nobody's.

C. Gas changed the scale rather than the idea. A network of pipes, a central works and a body of employees replaced individual lamps, and for the first time a city could be lit continuously rather than on nights when the moon was expected to fail. The effect on urban life was substantial and largely unanticipated: evening trade, evening entertainment and evening working hours all followed, and the boundary of the working day moved.

D. The claim made most often for lighting has been about crime, and the evidence for it is more mixed than either advocates or sceptics usually allow. Improved lighting is associated with reductions in some settings and with no measurable change in others, and the reductions occur during daylight hours as often as at night — a pattern that points to increased confidence and use of a space rather than to visibility at the moment of an offence.

E. What has been established more firmly concerns fear rather than crime. Lighting alters who is willing to use a street after dark, and that effect is large, consistent across studies and unequally distributed: it matters most to those who already restrict their movement, which is disproportionately women, older people and anyone whose route involves walking rather than driving. A street unused because it is frightening is a lost public asset whether or not anything ever happens on it.

F. The recent concern is the opposite of scarcity. Cheap efficient lamps have made light so inexpensive that the constraint on installing more has effectively gone, and the consequences — sky brightening, disrupted sleep, and effects on nocturnal insects and migrating birds — arrive from over-provision rather than under-provision. The design questions now are about direction, timing and colour rather than quantity, which is an unfamiliar way to think about a service that spent three centuries being scarce.

passages.title: What the Fungi Are Doing
passages.text:
Beneath a forest floor, the roots of most trees are wrapped in or penetrated by fungal threads. The association is ancient and near-universal: the fungus receives sugars the tree makes by photosynthesis, and the tree receives water and mineral nutrients that the fungal threads, far finer than any root, can extract from soil the root cannot reach. This much is settled, thoroughly demonstrated, and of considerable practical importance in forestry.

What has attracted public attention is a further claim: that these fungal threads connect separate trees into a network through which resources and even warnings pass, and that mature trees use it to support their offspring. The image is appealing, has been widely repeated, and rests on a body of evidence considerably thinner than its popularity suggests.

The demonstrated components should be separated from the inferred ones. That a single fungal individual can be physically connected to more than one tree is established. That labelled carbon injected into one tree can later be detected in another is also established. What does not follow is that the transfer occurred through the fungal connection rather than through soil, that the quantity is biologically meaningful to the receiving tree, or that the direction is anything other than incidental to the fungus's own interests.

Field evidence is scarce because the experiment is genuinely difficult. Severing connections without disturbing soil, roots and everything else is close to impossible; most supporting work comes from seedlings in containers, over short periods, under conditions unlike a forest. A recent systematic review of the field found that the claims most frequently cited in popular accounts were supported by a small number of studies, several of which did not report what they were said to report.

The interpretive difficulty runs deeper than the data. A fungus that moves carbon between trees is not being generous; it is managing its own supply, and framing the relationship as trees helping one another imports an intention that nothing in the system requires. The same observations are compatible with a fungus exploiting several hosts, and that reading is at least as consistent with what is measured.

None of this diminishes the association's importance, and the deflation is often taken further than the evidence warrants in that direction too. Fungal partners demonstrably determine which trees establish on which soils, how plantations perform, and how forests recover after disturbance. The case for taking soil fungi seriously in forest management is strong and does not depend on the network claim being true.

passages.title: Selling the Absence of Trouble
passages.text:
Insurance sells something no purchaser wants to use. The transaction converts an uncertain large loss into a certain small payment, and its value lies in that conversion rather than in any expected gain — over a lifetime the average purchaser pays more than they receive, and this is not evidence that the product is defective. A household that can absorb a small regular cost but not a catastrophic one is rationally better off after the exchange even though it is poorer on average.

The industry's two structural problems are worth stating plainly because they explain most of what looks arbitrary about its products. The first is that people who know they are at high risk are the keenest to buy, so a pool priced for average risk attracts worse-than-average customers and must raise prices, which drives the better risks out and repeats. The second is that being insured changes behaviour: a covered loss is a smaller loss, and some care is accordingly withdrawn.

Almost every feature that irritates customers exists to address one of these. Excesses and deductibles leave the purchaser exposed to a portion of every claim so that care is retained. Detailed questionnaires and medical histories exist to price the first problem rather than the second. Compulsory schemes solve the first outright by removing the choice to leave the pool, which is why insurance for driving, and health cover in many countries, is not voluntary.

The pooling that makes insurance work has a technical requirement often overlooked: losses must be substantially independent of one another. A fire in one house says little about the next; a flood, a windstorm or an earthquake affects thousands of policies at once, and correlated losses of that kind can exhaust reserves built for independent ones. Insurers manage this by passing risk to reinsurers and by geographic spread, and where correlation is severe enough the market withdraws.

That withdrawal is now the most consequential development in the sector. As losses from certain hazards become more frequent and more predictable, the risk stops being insurable in the ordinary sense — a near-certain loss cannot be pooled, only funded — and cover is priced upward or refused. The signal is economically useful, since it identifies where building should not continue, and politically intolerable, since it strands existing owners who bought under different assumptions.

The responses attempted have a common weakness. Public schemes that cap premiums or guarantee cover in withdrawn markets transfer the cost rather than reducing it, and by holding prices below risk they remove precisely the signal that would discourage further building in the exposed area. Schemes that pair support with restrictions on new construction perform better, and are correspondingly harder to legislate.
